pedagogy.summary: Using a simple formula means reading what it tells you to do — in words or symbols — substituting the given values, and computing with the correct order of operations, applying EVERY operation the formula specifies. The signature pitfalls are ignoring the bracket in P = 2(l + w) (doubling only the length), omitting the ½ in the area of a triangle, confusing the perimeter and area formulae, and mismatched units. Connecting each formula to the shape it describes keeps the computation meaningful.
bestPractices: Read the formula first and say what it computes and what each letter means before substituting.
Do the bracket first: for P = 2(l + w), add length and width, THEN double — not 2×l + w.
Apply every operation in the formula, including the ½ for a triangle; link it to the triangle being half its enclosing rectangle.
Distinguish perimeter (distance round, in cm) from area (space inside, in cm²) and attach the correct units.
Substitute carefully and check the result is sensible for the shape.
keyRepresentations: The shape itself with the formula overlaid (perimeter traced round the edge)
Triangle drawn inside its enclosing rectangle (why ½)
Function machine for the sequence of operations
commonMisconceptions: Ignores the bracket / order of operations: P = 2(l + w) computed as 2×l + w (e.g. 2×5+3 = 13 instead of 2×8 = 16).
Omits the ½ in a triangle's area, giving b×h (24) instead of ½×b×h (12).
Confuses perimeter and area formulae, or uses the wrong measurements.
Attaches wrong units (perimeter in cm², or no units).
Reads a worded formula incorrectly and mis-sequences the operations.

learn.summary: Year 6 learners use simple formulae (in words or symbols) to calculate values, substituting given numbers and applying EVERY operation in the correct order. The signature pitfalls are ignoring the bracket in P = 2(l + w) and doubling only the length (2×l + w), omitting the ½ in the area of a triangle, confusing perimeter with area, and mismatched units (cm vs cm²). Connecting each formula to the shape it describes keeps the computation meaningful.

activities.title: Formula-on-a-shape: watch the bracket do its work
feedback: If the 'double first' trace fails to close, point out that it counts both lengths but only one width, so it falls short by one width — the bracket (add first) is what makes the boundary close.

For the triangle, if the ½ is treated as optional, show that the leftover pieces of the same-base, same-height rectangle exactly cover the triangle (for a right-angled triangle, two identical copies form the rectangle): base × height is the whole rectangle, so the triangle's area is half of that. With a paper cut-out, treat it as a model of the ideal flat triangle.
When the answer looks wrong, prompt: 'read the formula again — have you done every operation it lists, in the order it lists them?'
activities.rationale: Seeing the bracket and the ½ act on an actual shape links symbolic order of operations to the quantity being measured, countering the instrumental, ungrounded learning that research associates with area/perimeter confusion and over-generalising the rectangle formula to triangles. Live recolouring, the perimeter trace, the function machine, and the 'double first' toggle are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; a static or paper version (tracing with a pen, cutting and rearranging a paper triangle against a rectangle with the same base and height) can carry the same idea, with the paper cut-out understood as an approximation of the ideal plane figure.
sourceClaims: Students writing/evaluating expressions apply operations left-to-right and mishandle the order of operations implied by symbolic form and parentheses — the same error that produces 2(l+w) -> 2*l+w.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae (A = l x b and P = 2(l + b)) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding (Van de Walle et al.; Dickson 1989: confusion is 'nearly always due to inadequate preparation... given the formulae without adequate explanation'); and they over-generalise the rectangle area formula, extending A = l x b to non-rectangular figures such as triangles (Olivier 1989) — the mechanism behind applying base x height to a triangle without the halving adjustment the triangle requires.
learnerActions: Set the length and width of a rectangle (for example with sliders), and evaluate P = 2(l + w) step by step: add length and width inside the bracket FIRST, then double.
Trace the perimeter round the edge of the rectangle as the formula computes, and check the traced path closes back on itself.
Toggle a 'double first' version that shows what 2×l + w would do — a path that traces both lengths but only one width, so it stops one side short and never closes round the shape.

Flip to a triangle whose top vertex lies above its base and place it on a rectangle with the same base and height (on screen or with a paper/card cut-out). Cut or drag the leftover pieces of the rectangle to show they exactly cover the triangle (for a right-angled triangle, two identical copies make the rectangle), so the ½ in A = ½ × b × h is seen as the triangle being half that rectangle. (A paper cut-out has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat, zero-thickness triangle; it still shows the half-area relationship.)
Optionally lay the formula out as a function machine so the sequence of operations the formula specifies is explicit.
State, in your own words, what each formula computes and what each letter means before substituting.
activities.intendedInsight: The bracket's order is not arbitrary here: adding-then-doubling walks the whole boundary and closes it, while doubling-then-adding misses one width and does not. The ½ for a triangle is the visible fact that a triangle has half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.

activities.title: Substitute and compute with feedback
feedback: If 13 appears for P (from 2×5 + 3), show that this doubles only the length; add length and width first, then double, to get 16 cm.
If 24 appears for the triangle, point to the ½ written in the formula — every operation must be carried out, so halve 24 to 12 cm².
If units are wrong (area with no square units, or perimeter in cm²), re-read what the formula computes: distance round (cm) versus space inside (cm²).
activities.rationale: Choosing formulae, substituting, and attaching units are cleanly checkable, and distractors built from the bracket and ½ errors make the characteristic mistakes visible for correction. A recognition/fill-in item checks substitution and formula choice but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify a full method; pair it with the step-showing and explanation actions above.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should use simple formulae (expressed in words or symbols) to calculate values.
Students writing/evaluating expressions apply operations left-to-right and mishandle the order of operations implied by symbolic form and parentheses — the same error that produces 2(l+w) -> 2*l+w.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: P = 2(5 + 3) = __, showing the bracket step (2 × 8 = 16 cm) before the answer.
Choose the area of a triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm from options including 12 cm² and the ½-omission result 24 cm²; explain why 24 is wrong.
Match each worded formula to its symbol form (e.g. 'multiply the base by the height, then halve' ↔ A = ½ × b × h).
Attach the correct units to each answer and say why perimeter is in cm but area is in cm².
Work an unfamiliar simple worded formula end-to-end, naming each operation as you do it.
activities.intendedInsight: Substituting into a given formula and picking the right formula/units is a procedure built by doing and checking; the common slips are the bracket and the dropped ½, so each is targeted directly.

activities.title: Label the shape and reveal the steps
feedback: If a learner cannot predict the next step, return to naming what each letter measures on the shape.
Use the revealed steps to confirm whether the bracket was handled first.
activities.rationale: A static labelled shape with step-reveal shows the parts of a formula clearly and supports reading it (in words or symbols) before use. It is a scaffold: because the numbers are fixed it does not let the learner compute across changing values, which is where the bracket and ½ errors actually surface, so follow it with the substitution and formula-on-a-shape activities.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should use simple formulae (expressed in words or symbols) to calculate values.
learnerActions: On a labelled rectangle, tap or point to the perimeter formula and reveal each step of the calculation in turn.
Say what each letter in the formula stands for on the drawing before any numbers are substituted.
Predict the next step before revealing it, then check your prediction against the shown calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Connecting each symbol to the part of the shape it measures keeps the formula meaningful before computing.

constraints: Perimeter and triangle area here are planar (2D) quantities; a third dimension is not needed and can mislead toward surface area or volume, so keep the representation flat.

A paper or card triangle cut out and rearranged against a rectangle with the same base and height has slight thickness and is an approximation of the ideal plane figure; use it to show the half-area relationship, not as a literal zero-thickness shape. This is also noted in the activity where the paper model is proposed.
The static label-and-reveal task is a scaffold: fixed numbers mean it cannot elicit computing across different values, which is where the characteristic errors live.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check substitution and formula/unit selection but do not on their own require the learner to construct and justify a full method; include step-showing and explanation to assess independent procedure.
Always apply every operation the formula specifies, in order: bracket first in P = 2(l + w), and include the ½ for a triangle.
Describe triangle area as half the base times the (perpendicular) height; avoid calling base and height 'two side lengths', since the height is a perpendicular distance, not necessarily a side.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: P = 2(5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 cm (bracket-ignoring slip gives 2×5 + 3 = 13); triangle area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm² (½-omission gives 6×4 = 24). All checked and consistent across the summary, activities, feedback, and constraints.

The source row's 3D-unsuitable and conversation-unsuitable ratings were catalog fit judgements; retained only the genuine, narrowly scoped point that a third dimension risks shifting toward surface area/volume for a planar quantity. No universal 'only this teaches' or 'dialogue cannot teach procedures' claim is asserted.

Source claim attributions were tightened: the curriculum-scope claim was removed from activity 1 because that activity's principle is conceptual grounding of order of operations/½, supported by the order-of-operations and area/perimeter claims rather than by curriculum scope.

The inherited worded formula 'multiply the two side lengths, then halve' loosely treated base and height as 'side lengths'; the learner-facing matching task was corrected to 'multiply the base by the height, then halve', since height is a perpendicular distance, not a triangle side. The original phrasing is recorded in the preservation audit for fidelity.

The cited sources support curriculum scope and the mechanisms of the order-of-operations and area/perimeter errors; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular activity or medium.

probeDeeper: In part (a), why add before you double? What do you get if you double first, and does it match the shape? (order-of-operations reasoning)
Your triangle sits inside a 6-by-4 rectangle — how do their areas compare, and why the ½? (counterexample/derivation for the half)
What units should each answer have, and why is area measured differently from perimeter?
Here is a formula in words: 'multiply the two side lengths, then halve.' Which is it — area of a triangle or perimeter of a rectangle? (interpreting a worded formula)

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the bracket / order of operations — computes 2(l + w) as 2×l + w, doubling only the length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bracket first — add length and width, THEN double; connect to perimeter as two lengths plus two widths traced round the shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2×5 + 3 = 13 (or similar); only one dimension is doubled before the other is added.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the ½ in a triangle's area — computes base × height and stops, giving the rectangle's area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the triangle as exactly half its enclosing rectangle by cutting/folding; stress that every operation written in the formula must be carried out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 24 (6×4) rather than 12; the ½ in the formula is not applied.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses perimeter and area, or the units — uses the wrong formula/quantity, or labels perimeter in cm².
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas — perimeter is the distance round (cm), area is the space inside (cm²); read what the formula computes before using it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds where the formula multiplies (or vice versa), or gives area with no square units / perimeter with cm².

responseLevels.gap: Ignores brackets/order or omits an operation (drops the ½), or selects the wrong formula; the calculation does not follow the formula as written.
responseLevels.full: Interprets worded or symbolic formulae, applies every operation in the correct order (bracket first, includes the ½), attaches correct units, and transfers the approach to an unfamiliar simple formula.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes and computes a single-operation formula correctly, but slips on the bracket in 2(l + w), forgets the ½, or muddles units — manages the routine case but not reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'work these out, showing your steps': (a) A rectangle has length 5 cm and width 3 cm — use P = 2(l + w) to find its perimeter. (b) A triangle has base 6 cm and height 4 cm — use A = ½ × b × h to find its area. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they do the bracket first in (a) and include the ½ in (b), and whether the units are right.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each item isolates an error in the written steps: (a) exposes ignoring the bracket (2×5+3 = 13) versus adding first then doubling (16); (b) exposes omitting the ½ (24) versus halving (12). Units (cm vs cm²) further separate a child who knows what each formula computes. Watching the steps, not asking, shows which operation was dropped or mis-ordered.
